subject: ss-haematology
title: Hereditary haemolysis membrane enzyme and oxidative defects
refs: Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine 22e Ch 105 Hemolytic Anemias
British Society for Haematology guideline on hereditary spherocytosis 2023

steps.tx: **Hereditary spherocytosis** (HS, membrane loss disease) is the commonest membrane defect, with incidence near **1** in **2000** in northern Europe and autosomal dominant spread in **75** percent. **Ankyrin** (anchor protein), band **3** (anion exchanger) and **spectrin** (membrane skeleton) mutations truncate the membrane, trapping water loss and spherocyte formation. **Osmotic fragility** (salt solution lysis test) picks it up, but **EMA binding** (eosin 5 maleimide binding test) is more specific.
steps.say: Hereditary spherocytosis is the commonest membrane defect and usually travels in families. Anchor protein mutations destroy membrane surface. EMA binding is more specific than osmotic fragility.

steps.tx: **Elliptocytosis** (oval membrane disease) follows **spectrin** or **protein 4.1** (membrane link protein) faults and often stays mild. **Stomatocytosis** (slit mouthed cells) arises from cation leaks, with hereditary and acquired forms, and overhydration marks the smear. **Acanthocytes** (spiculated cells) cluster in severe liver disease and **McLeod phenotype** (Kell system variant with chorea). Each shape whispers its protein fault.
steps.say: Elliptocytosis often stays mild despite striking oval cells. Stomatocytosis arises from cation leaks. Spiculated acanthocytes cluster in liver disease and the McLeod phenotype.

steps.tx: **G6PD deficiency** (glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase enzyme lack) is the commonest enzyme defect, X linked and affecting **400** million people. The **hexose monophosphate shunt** (oxidation protective pathway) makes **NADPH** (reducing power) and **glutathione** (antioxidant shield), which detoxify oxidants. Triggers include fava beans in **favism** (acute oxidative haemolysis), rasburicase, primaquine and nitrofurantoin, and cells show **bite** and **blister** damage.
steps.say: G6PD deficiency affects four hundred million people worldwide. Favism and oxidant drugs trigger acute haemolysis. Bite and blister cells mark oxidative damage on the smear.

steps.tx: **Pyruvate kinase deficiency** (PKD, final glycolysis enzyme fault) ranks second among enzyme defects and follows autosomal recessive inheritance. Red cells cannot make enough **ATP** (cell fuel) and suffer membrane failure. **Heinz bodies** (denatured haemoglobin clumps) appear in both G6PD and PKD, and **brilliant cresyl blue** stain reveals them. Neonatal jaundice is often the first clue, sometimes needing exchange transfusion.
steps.say: Pyruvate kinase deficiency ranks second among enzyme defects and follows recessive inheritance. Heinz bodies show denatured haemoglobin clumps. Neonatal jaundice is often the first presentation.

steps.tx: Haemolysis signature is shared: **jaundice** (yellow skin from bilirubin), dark urine, splenomegaly and anaemia with high **reticulocytes** (young red cells). **LDH** (lactate dehydrogenase) climbs while **haptoglobin** (haemoglobin binding protein) falls. **Urobilinogen** (bile pigment in urine) rises, while bilirubin stays **unconjugated** (water insoluble pigment). Symptom onset may be gradual over years in mild hereditary disease.
steps.say: Jaundice, splenomegaly and splenic enlargement mark chronic haemolysis. LDH rises while haptoglobin falls. Reticulocytes climb as the marrow compensates.

steps.tx: The **Coombs test** (direct antiglobulin test) stays negative in hereditary disease and positive in immune haemolysis, making it the opening fork. **Coagulation** studies and blood cultures help when microangiopathy looms. **Haemoglobin electrophoresis** (protein separation test) screens haemoglobinopathies. A ** Heinz body** screen and enzyme assay confirm oxidant defects, while membrane protein analysis settles membrane diagnoses.
steps.say: A negative Coombs test points away from immune haemolysis. Electrophoresis screens haemoglobinopathies. Enzyme and protein assays confirm membrane and enzyme faults.

steps.tx: **Splenectomy** (spleen removal) transforms severe spherocytosis and many enzyme defects by stopping premature splenic trapping, and it is delayed until after age **5** to protect vaccine response. Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus must precede surgery. **Folic acid** supports brisk marrow turnover. **Parvovirus B19** (red cell viral infection) can crash haemoglobin in chronic haemolysis, a crisis every student must recognise.
steps.say: Splenectomy transforms severe spherocytosis but is delayed beyond age five. Vaccination must precede the operation. Parvovirus infection can crash haemoglobin in chronic haemolysis.

steps.tx: Complications accumulate quietly. **Pigment gallstones** (bilirubin stones) fill the gallbladder in lifelong haemolysis, while **aplastic crises** follow parvovirus and **megaloblastic crises** follow folate shortage. Iron overload creeps with chronic transfusion. Iron chelators such as **deferasirox** (oral chelator) protect transfused patients, and hydroxyurea offers selected sickle cell benefit through **HbF** (fetal haemoglobin) induction.
steps.say: Pigment gallstones fill the gallbladder in lifelong haemolysis. Aplastic crisis follows parvovirus infection. Megaloblastic crisis follows folate shortage during brisk turnover.

steps.tx: Diagnosis now leans on sequencing. **NGS panels** (next generation sequencing gene tests) cover membrane and enzyme genes together and resolve atypical cases. Genetic counselling aids families, and prenatal diagnosis is possible in severe pedigrees. **Osmotic fragility** remains a screening tool where EMA binding is unavailable. Results guide splenectomy timing, trigger avoidance lists and reproductive advice.
steps.say: Gene panels now cover membrane and enzyme defects together. Genetic counselling aids families and prenatal diagnosis is possible. Osmotic fragility still screens where EMA binding is unavailable.

steps.tx: Anchors for the exam: spherocytes with negative Coombs equal hereditary spherocytosis; **G6PD** is X linked with bite cells and favism history; Heinz bodies show on brilliant cresyl blue; splenectomy after age **5** with vaccination is the rule; pigment gallstones mark chronic haemolysis; and parvovirus causes aplastic crisis. **EMA binding** beats osmotic fragility for spherocytosis confirmation.
steps.say: Spherocytes with a negative Coombs test equal hereditary spherocytosis. G6PD is X linked and triggered by fava beans. EMA binding beats osmotic fragility for confirmation.
